title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
This page demonstrates the estimators that py-qte offers for unconfounded data. All four estimators provide effects for the overall population (QTE) and for the treated group (QTT), but they differ in how they adjust for covariates:
For the covariate-adjusted estimators, the target argument selects the estimand: CausalTarget.QTE for the overall population or CausalTarget.QTT for the treated. For the unadjusted estimator, the two estimands coincide when treatment is randomly assigned.
The covariate-adjusted estimators rely on unconfoundedness and overlap: conditional on covariates \(X\), treatment is independent of the potential outcomes, and both treatment states occur with positive probability. The unadjusted estimator requires that the treatment is as good as randomly assigned. All estimators compute point estimates on the original sample and bootstrap standard errors by resampling rows.
The implementations are inspired by the R qte package.
Listing 1 displays the quantiles used throughout and the bootstrap configuration.
Listing 1


from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

QS = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)

title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
LaLonde Data
The LaLonde (1986) data are a standard example for covariate adjustment. We use the version that compares the treated men from the experimental sample with the observational PSID comparison group. The outcome is 1978 earnings (re78), the treatment is treat, and the covariates are age, education, race, marital status and degree status. The PSID comparison group is not randomly assigned, which is why the covariate-adjusted estimators below use it.



Listing 2


from qte.datasets import load_lalonde

COVARIATES = "age + I(age**2) + education + black + hispanic + married + nodegree"

DATA = load_lalonde(controls_source="psid").with_columns(pl.col("treat").cast(pl.Int8))
print(f"{DATA.height:,} observations, {DATA['treat'].sum():,} treated")

2,675 observations, 185 treated




Table 1 reports the mean of each variable by treatment status.

VARIABLES = {

title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
Unadjusted Estimator
The unadjusted estimator takes the difference between the treated and control quantiles at each requested probability,
\[
\hat{\Delta}_{\tau}
= \hat{Q}_{\tau}(Y \mid D = 1) - \hat{Q}_{\tau}(Y \mid D = 0),
\]
and reports the difference in means as the average effect. No propensity score or outcome model is involved.



Listing 3


from qte.unconfounded import estimate_unadjusted_effects

with timer("unadjusted"):
    unadjusted = estimate_unadjusted_effects(
        DATA,
        "re78",
        "treat",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,

title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
Inverse Probability Weighting
IPW estimates the counterfactual outcome distributions by weighting each observation with the inverse of its probability of receiving the treatment it actually received. With \(\hat{p}(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X)\), the distribution under treatment \(d\) is
\[
\hat{F}_{Y(d)}(y)
=
\frac{\sum_i \mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\}\,\mathbf{1}\{Y_i \le y\} / \hat{p}_d(X_i)}
     {\sum_i \mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\} / \hat{p}_d(X_i)},
\qquad
\hat{p}_1(X) = \hat{p}(X),\quad \hat{p}_0(X) = 1 - \hat{p}(X).
\]
propensity_score_formula specifies the logit model for \(\hat{p}(X)\). The target argument selects CausalTarget.QTE for the population or CausalTarget.QTT for the treated.



Listing 4


from qte.unconfounded import CausalTarget, estimate_ipw_effects

with timer("ipw"):
    ipw = estimate_ipw_effects(
        DATA,
        "re78",
        "treat",
        qs=QS,
        propensity_score_formula=COVARIATES,
        target=CausalTarget.QTE,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,

title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
Outcome Regression
Outcome regression fits a quantile regression of the outcome on the covariates separately for the treated and the control group. For a grid of quantiles \(\tau_g\), the fitted conditional quantiles \(\hat{Q}_{Y(d)}(\tau_g \mid X_i)\) generate a prediction for every unit. Pooling these predictions gives the counterfactual distribution
\[
\hat{F}_{Y(d)}(y)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}
\mathbf{1}\left\{\hat{Q}_{Y(d)}(\tau_g \mid X_i) \le y\right\}.
\]
The outcome_regression_config argument takes either a formula or an OutcomeRegressionConfig, which also controls the quantile grid and the quantile-regression algorithm.



Listing 5


from qte.unconfounded import estimate_outcome_regression_effects

with timer("outcome regression"):
    outcome_regression = estimate_outcome_regression_effects(
        DATA,
        "re78",
        "treat",
        qs=QS,
        outcome_regression_config=COVARIATES,

title: Unconfounded Estimators
text:
Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting
AIPW combines the two models. The propensity score reweights the observed outcomes, while the outcome regression predicts the outcomes that are not observed. For treatment state \(d\), the estimated counterfactual distribution is, up to normalization,
\[
\hat{F}_{Y(d)}(y)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
\frac{\mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\}\,\mathbf{1}\{Y_i \le y\}}{\hat{p}_d(X_i)}
-
\frac{\mathbf{1}\{D_i = d\} - \hat{p}_d(X_i)}{\hat{p}_d(X_i)}
\hat{F}_{Y(d)\mid X_i}(y)
\right].
\]
The estimator is doubly robust in the sense that it remains consistent if either the propensity score or the outcome regression is correctly specified. It takes both formulas, and the same target argument as IPW.



Listing 6


from qte.unconfounded import estimate_aipw_effects

with timer("aipw"):
    aipw = estimate_aipw_effects(
        DATA,
        "re78",
        "treat",
        qs=QS,
        propensity_score_formula=COVARIATES,
        outcome_regression_config=COVARIATES,
        target=CausalTarget.QTE,

title: perform_instrument_validity_test
text:
iv.perform_instrument_validity_test(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    outcome: ColumnName,
    treatment: ColumnName,
    instrument: ColumnName,
    *,
    weights: ColumnName | None = None,
    weighting: ValidityWeighting = ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE,
    se_floor: float = 0.15,
    outcome_grid_size: int = 50,
    alpha: float = 0.05,
    bootstrap_config: BootstrapConfig | int = 1000,
)
Test instrument validity with the Kitagawa (2015) test.
The treatment and the instrument need to be binary, and D = 1 needs to be the state that the instrument encourages (as of now you have to recode the variables if it is not).
The test relies on the fact that, under the assumptions that identify a treatment effect on the compliers, we must have
\[
P(B, 1) - Q(B, 1) >= 0 and
Q(B, 0) - P(B, 0) >= 0.
\]
That is, the distribution of \((Y,D)\) when the instrument is switched on (off), \(P\) (\(Q\)), assigns at least as much probability as the other one to every set \(B\) whenever the treatment is on (off).
The test builds a test statistic on this basis and then uses the pooled bootstrap to derive the distribution of the test statistic under the assumption that \(Q\) and \(P\) are in fact equal.
Notice that the test can only reject instrument validity, not confirm it. Further, the test is conservative in the sense that it tends to underreject. This is because the bootstrap distribution is computed at \(P = Q\), the least favourable member of the null, so the critical values are conservative whenever the inequalities are slack.
This implementation is relatively close to the original Kitagawa (2015) paper as opposed to the implementation in the ivcheck R package which uses the wild bootstrap.

Load the JTPA job-training data used in Abadie, Angrist & Imbens (2002).
The Job Training Partnership Act (JTPA) study randomly assigned applicants to a treatment group eligible for training or to a control group. The binary instrument assignmt records assignment, training records actual enrolment and earnings is total 30-month earnings. Non-compliance is almost entirely one-sided: only 54 of 3717 controls enrol in training. The data are the 11,204-observation extract distributed with the Stata ivqte documentation (Froelich & Melly, 2010).

datasets.load_ddk_2011()
Load the Duflo, Dupas and Kremer (2011) tracking dataset.
The data come from the randomized evaluation of tracking in Kenyan primary schools. The running variable is the student’s baseline test percentile, percentile; the cutoff is 50. In tracking schools, highstream indicates assignment to the upper-ability section, and ts_std is the standardized endline test score. The dataset is distributed with the R package QTE.RD and is the empirical example in Qu and Yoon (2025).

title: estimate_ivqr_effects
text:
iv.estimate_ivqr_effects(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    outcome: ColumnName,
    treatment: IvqrTreatment,
    instruments: ColumnName | Sequence[ColumnName],
    qs: ArrayLike = MEDIAN,
    *,
    covariates: FormulaRhs = '1',
    n_workers: int = 1,
)
Estimate an instrumental-variable quantile regression.
We estimate the structural quantile function
\[
q(\tau, d, x) = d' \alpha(\tau) + x' \beta(\tau).
\]
For a unit with covariates \(x\) and treatment \(d\), this describes the \(\tau\)-quantile of the potential outcome \(Y(d)\). It is assumed that \(d\) is endogenous, which is why it needs to be instrumented.
The estimation procedure requires an IvqrTreatment, which supplies the treatment column and the grid for \(\alpha\) at which the objective function is evaluated. Notice that we only allow for a single treatment as multiple \(d\) would make the procedure prohibitively slow.
Standard errors are computed analytically. The procedure is still computationally demanding: for each \(\tau\), a quantile regression must be run for every value in the treatment grid. Again, for this reason we do not allow multiple treatments.
The mean effect reported in att is the average of the estimated quantile treatment effects. For this to be interpretable as a full-distribution average, the \(\tau\) grid should be dense. A standard two-stage least squares estimate is also reported in tsls. There is no reason for the mean of the quantiles and the two-stage least squares estimate to coincide, since they refer to different causal targets.
Finally, the estimator targets the quantile treatment effect. This is a population-level structural effect, not a local complier effect.

distributional_did.estimate_distributional_did_effects(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    outcome: ColumnName,
    treatment_group: ColumnName | TrtGroupConfig,
    time: ColumnName,
    unit: ColumnName,
    qs: ArrayLike = MEDIAN,
    *,
    weights: ColumnName | None = None,
    n_anticipation_periods: int = 0,
    base_period: BasePeriod = BasePeriod.UNIVERSAL,
    control_group: ControlGroup = ControlGroup.NEVER_TREATED,
    bootstrap_config: BootstrapConfig | int = 1000,
)
Estimate quantile treatment effects with distributional difference-in-differences.
Combines a distributional parallel trends assumption – the distribution of the change in untreated potential outcomes is the same for the treated and untreated groups – with the assumption that the dependence, that is the copula, between the change in untreated potential outcomes and the initial level of untreated potential outcomes is the same for the two groups. The initial distribution of outcomes is allowed to differ between the groups, which is what distinguishes this estimator from quantile difference-in-differences, where the unobservables must be identically distributed everywhere. The counterfactual pairs each control unit’s own change over time with the treated outcome at that unit’s rank, so it needs the same units in both periods of a cell, and it is indexed on the control units, which means the distribution of individual treatment effects is not identified. Returns the group, event-study, overall and group-time effects.

title: Instrument Validity
text:
The local quantile treatment effects on the estimators page require the instrument to be valid. The py-qte package implements the Kitagawa 2015 test for instrument validity.
For a binary treatment \(D\) and a binary instrument \(Z\), let \(P\) denote the distribution of \((Y, D)\) when the instrument is switched on and \(Q\) the distribution when it is switched off. Under the LATE assumptions of Imbens & Angrist 1994, every set \(B\) must satisfy
\[
P(B, 1) - Q(B, 1) \ge 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
Q(B, 0) - P(B, 0) \ge 0,
\]
because both differences are probabilities of a complier’s potential outcome falling in \(B\). the py-qte package implements Kitagawa’s test based on these inequalities. The implementation is inspired by the original paper and the related R ivcheck package; unlike ivcheck, it uses Kitagawa’s pooled bootstrap rather than a wild bootstrap.

title: Instrument Validity
text:
The Test Statistic
The test evaluates the inequalities over intervals of the outcome. For each interval and treatment value it computes the violation of the corresponding inequality; the test statistic is the largest violation. With ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE, each violation is divided by its plug-in standard error before the maximum is taken, which is the statistic in equation 2.1 of Kitagawa 2015. With ValidityWeighting.UNWEIGHTED, the raw violation is used instead (equation 2.2).
Critical values come from a pooled bootstrap. Replications are drawn from the pooled empirical distribution of \((Y, D)\), which imposes the null that the two instrument arms have the same distribution. The p-value is the share of bootstrap statistics at least as large as the observed one.



Listing 1


from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

VALIDITY_BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=200, seed=42, n_workers=4)

jtpa = load_jtpa().filter(pl.col("sex") == 0)
print(f"{jtpa.height} women")

title: Instrument Validity
text:
Subdensities
Listing Listing 3 shows how to construct the Kitagawa-style joint subdensities \(p(y, d \mid z)\) separately for the two instrument arms and treatment values. These are the distributions behind the inequalities above: under validity, the instrument-on distribution should place at least as much mass as the instrument-off distribution on every interval when \(d = 1\), and vice versa when \(d = 0\). The figure is a descriptive complement to the formal test, not a test itself.



Listing 3


from qte.iv.descriptives import make_subdensity_plot

subdensities = make_subdensity_plot(
    jtpa,
    "earnings",
    "training",
    "assignmt",
    labels={
        "earnings": "Earnings",
        "training": "Training",
        "assignmt": "Assignment",
    },
    title="JTPA earnings subdensities by assignment and training status",
).configure_legend(orient="bottom")




show_chart(subdensities)






Figure 1: JTPA earnings subdensities by assignment and training status.




The figure lines up with the validity inequalities: in the training panel the assigned arm lies above the unassigned arm, while the reverse holds in the no-training panel.

title: Instrument Validity
text:
Running the Test
perform_instrument_validity_test uses ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE by default. This standardizes each interval violation by its plug-in standard error before taking the maximum, which is the statistic in equation 2.1 of Kitagawa 2015. We use this version because it accounts for the different sampling variability of the interval probabilities. The alternative, ValidityWeighting.UNWEIGHTED, uses the raw positive-part Kolmogorov–Smirnov violation instead (equation 2.2). The se_floor argument bounds the plug-in standard error from below, and outcome_grid_size controls the number of outcome grid points used in the interval search.

from qte.iv import ValidityWeighting, perform_instrument_validity_test

with timer("validity"):
    validity_test = perform_instrument_validity_test(
        jtpa,
        "earnings",
        "training",
        "assignmt",
        weighting=ValidityWeighting.VARIANCE,
        bootstrap_config=VALIDITY_BOOTSTRAP,
    )

title: Aggregating Estimates
text:
All estimators in qte.distributional_did follow the per-cell approach of Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021: for a treatment group \(g\) and a period \(t\) they construct the counterfactual distribution of that cell and compare it to the observed one. We are often interested in effects above the level of the individual cells. In the py-qte package, besides the cell-level effect estimates, effects by treatment group, by event time and overall effects, all on the treated, are available.
In the following, we demonstrate these aggregations using the mpdta dataset, a description of which can be found here in the context of the Changes-in-Changes (CIC) estimator.
Listing 1 shows the estimation on which our aggregations are based.
Listing 1


from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig
from qte.datasets import load_mpdta
from qte.distributional_did import estimate_changes_in_changes_effects

QS = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]

# Kept deliberately small so the page builds quickly while the documentation is being iterated on.
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)

panel = load_mpdta().with_columns(pl.col("first.treat").replace(0, float("inf")).alias("group"))

with timer("changes-in-changes"):
    cic = estimate_changes_in_changes_effects(
        panel,
        "lemp",
        "group",
        "year",
        "countyreal",
        qs=QS,
        bootstrap_config=BOOTSTRAP,
    )

title: Aggregating Estimates
text:
Aggregation
Aggregating distributional estimates differs from aggregating means. To get from cell-level means to an aggregation level of choice, it is enough to weight the individual cells by their relative cell sizes. This is not true for the aggregation of quantiles: a sum of cell-size-weighted quantiles generally does not correspond to the quantile of the distribution that corresponds to the aggregation level (for instance, the overall distribution of outcomes under treatment and under no treatment for the treated group). Thus, one first has to construct the aggregate distribution by combining the cell-level distributions (on a common grid) with the appropriate weights; the quantiles of interest are then the quantiles of that aggregate distribution.

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
This page demonstrates the estimators that py-qte offers for distributional difference-in-differences. The available estimators are
All four follow the approach of Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021 in that they allow an arbitrary number of groups and time periods, but the actual effects are estimated per treated group-time cell relative to a single comparison (pre-treatment) period and a single control group. The estimators offer various ways to determine the comparison group and period. As in Callaway & Sant’Anna 2021, aggregation procedures are offered which give treatment effects at higher levels than the individual group-time cells of the treated. The available aggregations are described here.
The object of interest in what follows is the entire distribution of \(Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=T)\), i.e. the potential outcome under no treatment (as indicated by the superscript \(d=0\)) for a group that was in fact treated, i.e. \(d=1\), at period \(T\).
The available estimators differ in under what assumptions this counterfactual distribution is derived from observables. The following sections give a brief description of each estimator and the underlying identification assumptions, together with showing how the corresponding estimation can be performed with the py-qte package and how to present the results.
Listing 1 displays what quantiles are computed throughout and the configuration of the boostrap.
Listing 1


from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

QS = [0.25, 0.50, 0.75]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
The Data
The demonstration data are county-level teen employment in the United States from 2003 to 2007, together with whether a county’s minimum wage was raised above the federal minimum. The dataset contains three treatment groups identified by the year in which the respective county was initially treated (2004, 2006, 2007). There is also a group of counties that was never treated. The panel is balanced: 500 counties observed in each of the five years.
The outcome of interest is lemp, the natural logarithm of the number of employed teenagers in the county. Because it is a count and not a rate, its level also reflects how large a county is, and differences in county size across the treatment groups are visible in the averages below.

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
Changes-in-Changes
The Changes-in-Changes (CIC) model was developed by Athey & Imbens 2006. The crucial assumptions are that the outcomes under no treatment — if the causal target of interest is an effect on the treated — are determined by a “production function”, \(Y^{d=0}=h(U,t)\), that depends on time, \(t\), and on a single unobserved index of individual-level characteristics, \(U\).
The production function is assumed to be monotone in that index, and it is indexed by neither group membership nor the individual observation \(i\). The distribution of \(U\) is unrestricted across groups but, within a group, does not change over time. It is further assumed that the latent characteristics satisfy a common support assumption across groups.
So this model, intuitively, assumes that in the absence of the treatment two individuals from different groups with the same latent characteristic \(U=u\) display the exact same evolution of outcomes. This, together with the assumption of common support, suggests that one can indeed identify the counterfactual distribution of the outcomes of the treated under no treatment in the post-treatment period.
Formally, under the assumptions of the CIC model this counterfactual distribution is generated by the following transformation, applied to the outcomes of the treated in the pre-treatment period.
\[
k_{CIC}(y) = F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}\!\left(F_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(y)\right).
\]

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
Quantile Difference-in-Differences
The Quantile Difference-in-Differences (QDID) model is motivated by the idea that the observed evolution of a quantile \(q\) of the (marginal) distribution of outcomes that the untreated experienced from the pre- to the post-treatment period can act as a stand-in for the counterfactual evolution of the same quantile that the outcome distribution of the treated would have experienced had they not been treated.
\[
F^{-1}_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}(q) =
F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(q) +
\left[F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}(q) - F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(q)\right]
\]
The QDID model is formalized — that is, connected to a set of assumptions on primitives — in Athey & Imbens 2006, Section 3.3. They assume that \(Y^{d=0} = \tilde{h}(U,G,T) = \tilde{h}_G(U,G) + \tilde{h}_T(U,T)\), which is strictly increasing in \(U\), and that \(U\) is independent of both \(G\) and \(T\). This model generates differences in the distribution of \(Y^{d=0}\) both across groups and across time. Intuitively, at a fixed \(U\) the change in untreated potential outcomes is identical across the two groups, which is what identifies the counterfactual distribution in an essentially analogous way to the standard difference-in-differences model (at a fixed \(u\) the counterfactual post-treatment period outcome of the treatment is exactly equal to the pre-treatment period outcome plus the observed change in the outcome derived from the untreated).
Applied to each treated pre-treatment outcome rather than to one quantile at a time, the identity above gives the following transformation:
\[
k_{QDID}(y) = y + \left[F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=1)}(q) - F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=0,t=0)}(q)\right],
\qquad q = F_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(y).
\]

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
Mean Difference-in-Differences
Mean Difference-in-Differences (MDID) shifts the treated group’s whole pre-treatment distribution by the change in the comparison group’s mean:
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) &= F_{Y,\text{pre}\mid D=1}(y - \Delta), \\[2pt]
\Delta &= E[Y_{\text{post}} \mid D=0] - E[Y_{\text{pre}} \mid D=0].
\end{aligned}
\]
This is stronger than the usual difference-in-differences assumption, which only requires the means to move in parallel: here every quantile of the counterfactual distribution is the corresponding pre-treatment quantile shifted by the same constant, \(F^{-1}_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}(q) = F^{-1}_{Y^{obs}(d=1,t=0)}(q) + \Delta\). In the notation of Athey & Imbens 2006 this is the transformation \(k_{DID}(y) = y + E[Y_{01}] - E[Y_{00}]\).
Relative to the QDID model, the change is not allowed to vary with \(u\): in the QDID model above the time effect can differ across quantiles, whereas here it is a single number. The quantile effects this model reports are consequently not evidence about how effects vary across the distribution — they are the treated group’s own distributional change net of a constant, and only the average effect rests on the identifying assumption.

title: Distributional Difference-in-Differences
text:
Distributional Difference-in-Differences
The Distributional Difference-in-Differences (DDiD) model of Callaway, Li & Oka 2018 assumes that the change in untreated potential outcomes has the same distribution in both groups. This, however, is not enough to identify \(F_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=1)}\). Intuitively, for a given pre-treatment period distribution of outcomes for the treated, \(F_{Y^{d=0}(d=1,t=0)}\), a restriction on the distribution of changes can generate many distributions of the outcome levels of the treated group in the post-treatment period. This issue can be remedied by imposing that the pre-treatment period levels and the changes from the pre- to the post-treatment period move in a similar way together in the treated and in the untreated group. Technically, it is required that the associated copula be the same in both groups.
The counterfactual distribution of interest is then given by:
\[
F_{Y(0)\mid D=1}(y) =
\Pr\left\{\Delta Y_{j} + F^{-1}_{Y_{10}}\!\left(F_{Y_{00}}(Y_{j})\right) \le y \;\middle|\; D = 0\right\},
\]
where \(\Delta Y_j\) is comparison unit \(j\)’s own change and \(Y_j\) its pre-treatment outcome.

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
This page demonstrates the instrumental-variable estimators in py-qte. All three estimate effects of an endogenous treatment, which is why they require an instrument.
The unconditional and conditional local quantile treatment effect estimators are similar in spirit to the local average treatment effect (LATE) of Imbens & Angrist 1994 in that they generally identify an effect on the complier subpopulation when the standard LATE assumptions hold. They also require a binary instrument and a binary treatment. The instrumental-variable quantile regression (IVQR) estimator estimates a population-level structural quantile effect in a framework in which the researcher must specify a structural quantile function.
Throughout the page we use different datasets to demonstrate the mechanics of the py-qte package for IV estimation. For the binary-instrument, binary-treatment case, we also show how the package produces useful descriptive statistics.
The implementations are inspired by the Stata ivqte package. The IVQR routine additionally follows the R IVQR package.
Listing 1 displays the quantiles used throughout and the bootstrap configuration.
Listing 1


from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig

QS = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90]
BOOTSTRAP = BootstrapConfig(n_iter=50, seed=42, n_workers=4)

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
Local (Quantile) Treatment Effects
The object of interest is the local quantile treatment effect (LQTE) for compliers. At quantile \(\tau \in (0, 1)\), it is defined as
\[
\Delta_\tau = Q_\tau(Y(1)\mid c) - Q_\tau(Y(0)\mid c),
\]
where \(Q_\tau(Y(d)\mid c)\) is the \(\tau\)-quantile of the potential outcome \(Y(d)\) in the complier subpopulation. The corresponding LATE is the difference in means, \(E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid c]\). Both the conditional and the unconditional LQTE estimators assume that the standard LATE assumptions hold conditional on covariates:

Independence: \(Z \perp (Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1)) \mid X\).
Exclusion: \(Y(z, d) = Y(d)\) for \(z \in \{0, 1\}\).
Monotonicity: \(D(1) \ge D(0)\) almost surely.
Relevance: \(E[D \mid Z = 1, X] \ne E[D \mid Z = 0, X]\).

Here \(D(z)\) is the potential treatment under instrument value \(z\), and \(Y(z, d)\) is the potential outcome under instrument value \(z\) and treatment value \(d\). Both estimators use Abadie’s kappa weights (Abadie 2003) to identify transformations of potential outcomes in the subpopulation of compliers. Testable implications of these assumptions for a binary instrument and a binary treatment are discussed on the instrument-validity page.

Unconditional Local Quantile Treatment Effects
The unconditional LQTE is the LQTE defined above, i.e. the effect is not conditional on covariates. We thus require the potential outcomes’ cumulative distribution function, which is the inverse of \(Q_\tau(\cdot \mid c)\):
\[
F_{Y(d)\mid c}(y) = \frac{E\!\left[w_d\,\mathbb{1}\{Y \le y\}\right]}{E[w_d]}
\]
where Abadie’s kappa weights are given by
\[
w_1 = \frac{D\,\bigl(Z - p(X)\bigr)}{p(X)\,\bigl(1 - p(X)\bigr)},
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
w_0 = \frac{(1 - D)\,\bigl(p(X) - Z\bigr)}{p(X)\,\bigl(1 - p(X)\bigr)}.
\]
Here \(p(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)\) is the instrument probability.
A general problem here is that the empirical CDFs might not be monotone. One must therefore specify how to deal with this non-monotonicity. In this setting, one can either use the original weights given above and impose an ad hoc rule for the value corresponding to a particular quantile of the possibly non-monotone empirical CDF, or project the weights on the outcome and the treatment to make them positive.
The following section demonstrates how to conduct an analysis with this estimator using the py-qte package.

Card (1995) Data
The Card (1995) data consist of 3,010 men from the 1976 National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men. The dataset can be used to study the effect of education on labour market outcomes, using whether the man grew up in close proximity to a college as an instrument. The instrument nearc4 indicates whether a man grew up in a local labour market with a four-year college, and the outcome of interest lwage is the log wage. The treatment is a binary indicator for having at least 13 years of education, i.e. some college. Following Tübbicke 2023, who in turn follows Słoczyński 2021, the estimation sample restricts the data to covariate cells with at least five observations. A cell is one of the observed combinations of black, south66, south, smsa66 and smsa; this drops 22 observations and leaves 2,988. Listing 2 shows how to load the dataset and produce a table of descriptive statistics with the py-qte package.



Listing 2


from qte.datasets import load_card
from qte.iv.descriptives import make_descriptive_statistics

CARD_CELLS = ["black", "south66", "south", "smsa66", "smsa"]
CARD_COVARIATES = (
    "exper + expersq + black + south + smsa + smsa66 "
    "+ reg662 + reg663 + reg664 + reg665 + reg666 + reg667 + reg668 + reg669"
)

sample = load_card(treatment_cutoff=13)
card = sample.filter(pl.len().over(CARD_CELLS) >= 5)
print(f"{sample.height} observations, {sample.height - card.height} dropped, {card.height} left")

card_desc = make_descriptive_statistics(
    card,
    "lwage",
    "college",

Conditional Local Quantile Treatment Effects
The conditional LQTE estimator of Abadie, Angrist & Imbens 2002 postulates
\[
Q_{\theta}(Y \mid X, D, c) = \alpha_{\theta} D + X' \beta_{\theta},
\]
where \(\alpha_{\theta}\) and \(\beta_{\theta}\) can be obtained via weighted quantile regression with Abadie’s kappa weights. Under the maintained assumptions, \(\alpha_{\theta}\) corresponds to the conditional (on covariate values) LQTE. Notice that, even though the conditional LQTE is assumed to be constant across covariates, it does not generally correspond to the unconditional LQTE. This is because integrating out the covariates from the conditional quantiles does not give the marginal quantile in general.
Generally, the sample version of the above quantile regression problem is difficult to solve because Abadie’s kappa weights can be negative, which makes the problem non-convex. The paper shows that this can be remedied by replacing the weights with their conditional expectation given \(U = (Y, D, X)\), which is guaranteed to be nonnegative and still identifies \(\alpha\) via weighted quantile regression as described above. In particular, these weights are given by
\[
\kappa_\nu(U) = E[\kappa \mid U]
= 1 - \frac{D\,\bigl(1 - \nu_0(U)\bigr)}{1 - p(X)}
  - \frac{(1 - D)\,\nu_0(U)}{p(X)},
\]
where
\[
\nu_0(U) = E[Z \mid U] = P(Z = 1 \mid Y, D, X),
\qquad U = (Y, D, X),
\]
and \(p(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)\) is the instrument probability.

title: Instrumental Variables
text:
Instrumental-Variable Quantile Regression
The model underlying the instrumental-variable quantile regression (IVQR) estimator was developed by Chernozhukov & Hansen 2004. The model assumes that potential outcomes are generated in accordance with \(Y(d) = q(d, X, U_d)\). The function \(q\) is nondecreasing in \(U_d\), and \(U_d \sim U(0, 1)\). Conditional on covariates \(X\), \(U_d\) is independent of \(Z\). Selection into treatment is determined in accordance with \(D = \delta(Z, X, V)\). Conditional on \((Z, X, V)\), the \(\{U_d\}\) are identically distributed (rank similarity), and the observed data are \(Y\), \(D\), \(X\) and \(Z\).
For this set of assumptions one can show that
\[
P[Y \le q(D, X, \tau) \mid X, Z] = \tau.
\]
This is essentially a conditional moment restriction that can be used to estimate quantile treatment effects.
In particular, following Chernozhukov & Hansen 2005 and 2006, the py-qte package assumes that
\[
q_\tau(Y \mid D = d, X = x) = d' \alpha(\tau) + x' \beta(\tau).
\]
Here again, \(\alpha\) corresponds to the treatment effect under the maintained assumptions.
The parameters \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) can be estimated via inverse quantile regression. For each quantile \(\tau\) and each candidate value of \(\alpha\) on a user-supplied grid, the outcome is shifted to \(Y - D\alpha\), the treatment is replaced by its first-stage fitted value, and a conventional quantile regression is run on the fitted treatment and the covariates. The selected \(\alpha\) then minimizes the Wald statistic for the coefficient on the fitted treatment, which reflects the exclusion restriction that the instrument \(Z\) does not directly influence outcomes. Notice that the algorithm generally requires, for each \(\tau\), one quantile regression per grid point for \(\alpha\). Each quantile regression has as parameters the fitted treatment and the covariates. The algorithm therefore tends to be computationally demanding, even though the standard errors are obtained analytically.
Notice that the py-qte implementation is less general than the model. We allow only a single treatment variable, whereas the model can accommodate multiple treatment variables. The algorithm would quickly run into the curse of dimensionality with multiple treatments because the number of grid points to search over grows exponentially. The implementation does, however, allow multiple instruments.

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
This page demonstrates how to use the py-qte package to obtain quantile treatment effects in the context of the regression-discontinuity design (RDD). The point estimator follows Frandsen, Frölich & Melly 2012 and targets quantile treatment effect for local compliers at the cutoff. It handles both sharp and fuzzy RDDs.
Under the standard RD assumptions, the distribution of the treated potential outcome among compliers at the cutoff is identified through the following Wald ratio
\[
F_{Y(1)\mid C}(y)
=
\frac{
\lim_{r\downarrow c} E[1(Y \le y) D \mid R = r]
-
\lim_{r\uparrow c} E[1(Y \le y) D \mid R = r]
}{
\lim_{r\downarrow c} E[D \mid R = r]
-
\lim_{r\uparrow c} E[D \mid R = r]
},
\]
and the control counterpart is the reverse side difference of \(1(Y \le y)(1-D)\). The quantile treatment effect is then the difference between the inverses of these two complier distribution functions.
Standard errors can be obtained via the case or the multiplier-bootstrap. The multiplier-bootstrap allows for the computation of uniform confidence bands, i.e. confidence bands that apply to all quantiles jointly.
The multiplier-bootstrap uniform band follows the constant-width convention of Chiang, Hsu & Sasaki 2019 and Stata’s rdqte package. The R package QTE.RD of Qu & Yoon 2025 also served as a reference point.
A bandwidth must be supplied. The estimator, as of now, does not select one internally. outcome_grid is either the number of weighted-quantile points used for the distribution regressions or an explicit sequence of outcome values.
from qte.bootstrap import BootstrapConfig, BootstrapMultiplierConfig
from qte.datasets import load_ddk_2011
from qte.rdd import (
    LocalPolynomialConfig,

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
The Data
The data are from Duflo, Dupas & Kremer 2011, a randomized evaluation of tracking in Kenyan primary schools. The paper asks whether separating students into high- and low-ability sections (“tracking”) improves learning, and how peer composition and teacher incentives, both changing with tracking, shape that answer. The authors have access to control schools without tracking. The setting, however, lends itself also to an RDD since within the tracking schools students where assigned to a track based on a cutoff in a baseline test score. The RDD setup, thus, can speak to a question regarding the effect of placing a marginal student into the track of better performing students. It is the empirical example in Qu & Yoon 2025
The main variables are:

percentile: the student’s baseline test percentile, the running variable.
highstream: assignment to the upper-ability section in a tracking school.
ts_std: the standardized endline test score, the outcome.
tracking: whether the school was sampled for tracking.

We keep the 2,980 tracking-school students with non-missing outcome and running variable, set the cutoff at 50, and define treatment sharply as being at or above the median percentile. The raw highstream variable is not perfectly deterministic at the cutoff, so the sharp definition keeps the demonstration focused on assignment at the cutoff. The dataset is the one distributed with the R package QTE.RD; the Stata benchmark uses the same sample and cutoff.



Listing 1


DDK = (
    load_ddk_2011()
    .filter(pl.col("tracking") == 1)
    .drop_nulls(["ts_std", "percentile"])
    .with_columns((pl.col("percentile") >= 50.0).cast(pl.Int64).alias("treatment"))
)
print(f"{DDK.height:,} students in tracking schools")
print(f"{DDK['treatment'].sum():,} at or above the median percentile")

title: Regression Discontinuity Design
text:
Uniform Bands
The RDD distribution estimator is the first and only design in py-qte that implements the multiplier boostrap, and therefore the only one that supports uniform confidence bands.
A pointwise interval covers the QTE at one quantile at a time:
\[
P\left(\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)-z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{se}(\tau)
\le \mathrm{QTE}(\tau)\le
\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)+z_{1-\alpha/2}\,\widehat{se}(\tau)\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
A uniform band covers the entire quantile curve simultaneously:
\[
P\left(\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}
\left|\widehat{\mathrm{QTE}}(\tau)-\mathrm{QTE}(\tau)\right|
\le c_{1-\alpha}\right)=1-\alpha.
\]
This is the relevant object when the whole QTE process is inspected, because it accounts for the joint variation across quantiles. The multiplier draws approximate the distribution of that process; the critical value is taken from the supremum across quantiles and draws.
Passing a BootstrapMultiplierConfig switches to multiplier draws. With degree=2 this is the CHS-style local-quadratic fit. The pointwise SEs and the uniform critical value come from the same draws. band="sup-t" uses the studentised sup-t critical value; band="uniform" uses the CHS/Stata constant-width band.

uniform_res = estimate_rdd_distribution_effects(
    DDK,
    outcome="ts_std",
    treatment="treatment",
    running_variable=RunningVariableConfig("percentile", 50.0),
    qs=QS,
    local_polynomial_config=LocalPolynomialConfig(bandwidth=20.0, degree=2),
    outcome_grid=200,
    bootstrap_config=UNIFORM_BOOTSTRAP,
)

text:
iv.estimate_conditional_local_effects(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    outcome: ColumnName,
    treatment: ColumnName,
    instrument: ColumnName,
    qs: ArrayLike = MEDIAN,
    *,
    covariates: FormulaRhs,
    weight_formula: FormulaRhs | None = None,
    instrument_probability_formula: FormulaRhs | None = None,
    weight_adjustment: WeightAdjustment = WeightAdjustment.PROJECTION,
    weights: ColumnName | None = None,
    trim: float = _DEFAULT_TRIM,
    bootstrap_config: BootstrapConfig | int = 100,
)
Estimate conditional quantile treatment effects for compliers as in Abadie et al. (2002).
The model postulates that \(Q_{\theta}(Y \mid X, D, D_{1} > D_{0}) = \alpha_{\theta} D + X' \beta_{\theta}\). \(\theta\) indexes the quantile of \(Y\). \(D\) is binary, one-dimensional and endogenous, which is why it needs to be instrumented.
\(\alpha\) can, in principle, be obtained from the following quantile regression problem: \[
(\alpha_{\theta}, \beta_{\theta})
= \arg\min_{\alpha, \beta} E\big[\kappa \, \rho_{\theta}(Y - \alpha D - X' \beta)\big],
\]
where \(\kappa\) is the signed Abadie’s kappa weight (\(\kappa = 1 - \frac{D\,(1 - Z)}{1 - \pi_0(X)} - \frac{(1 - D)\,Z}{\pi_0(X)}\) with \(\pi_0(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)\)). This problem is computationally challenging since the weights can be negative. Thus, the weights are replaced with another set of weights, where \(U = (Y, D, X)\) and \(\nu_0(U) = E[Z \mid U]\):
\[
\tilde{\kappa}(U) = E[\kappa \mid U]
= 1 - \frac{D\,(1 - \nu_0(U))}{1 - \pi_0(X)}
  - \frac{(1 - D)\,\nu_0(U)}{\pi_0(X)},
\]
which can be shown to be nonnegative across the board. The weight_formula gives the design of the first step and weight_adjustment the way it is used: PLUGIN approximates \(\nu_0(U)\) and plugs it into the identity above, PROJECTION projects \(\kappa\) on the design directly.
Standard errors are found via a case bootstrap.
The estimand is the coefficient on the treatment in a quantile regression of the outcome on the treatment and the covariates, for compliers. Notice that the conditional (on \(X\)) effect (on the compliers) generally does not coincide with the unconditional effect (on the compliers). This is because here we identify \(Q_{\theta}(Y \mid D=1, X=x) - Q_{\theta}(Y \mid D=0, X=x) = \alpha_{\theta}\) (for the compliers), but if we integrate out \(X\) on the left hand side, the resulting functional is not comprised of the marginal distributions of \(Y\) given the treatment status for the compliers, since quantiles are not linear operators.

The counterfactual distribution of untreated potential outcomes for the treated group is the treated group’s pre-treatment distribution shifted by the change in the control group’s mean. This implies the usual parallel trends assumption, so the average treatment effect on the treated is identified, but it is stronger: it also requires that only the location of the distribution shifts, not its shape. The quantile treatment effects that follow, Q(Y | treated, post) - Q(Y | treated, pre) - delta, are a mechanical consequence of that shape restriction: they vary across quantiles only because the treated group’s own distribution moves over time, which the assumption leaves unrestricted. Their shape therefore says nothing about how treatment effects vary, and only the average effect rests on the identifying assumption. Returns the group, event-study, overall and group-time effects.

iv.estimate_unconditional_local_effects(
    ds: pl.DataFrame,
    outcome: ColumnName,
    treatment: ColumnName,
    instrument: ColumnName,
    qs: ArrayLike = MEDIAN,
    *,
    instrument_probability_formula: FormulaRhs | None = None,
    weights: ColumnName | None = None,
    trim: float = _DEFAULT_TRIM,
    estimator: Estimator = Estimator.SIGNED,
    bootstrap_config: BootstrapConfig | int = 100,
)
Estimate the local quantile treatment effect for compliers.
The causal target is the difference between the complier quantiles of the treated and untreated potential outcomes. It is a local effect analogous to the local average treatment effect (LATE), but for quantiles rather than means. Notice further, that the effect is unconditional in the sense that it is not conditional on covariate values but rather applies to the population (of compliers) as a whole.
The effect is obtained using Abadie’s kappa weights:
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_1 &= \frac{D Z}{p(X)} - \frac{D (1 - Z)}{1 - p(X)}, \\
w_0 &= \frac{(1 - D)(1 - Z)}{1 - p(X)} - \frac{(1 - D) Z}{p(X)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(p(X) = P(Z = 1 \mid X)\), so a formula for the instrument propensity should be supplied.
The weights are not necessarily positive. The estimator argument controls how negative weights are handled. With Estimator.SIGNED, negative weights are retained, which can lead to non-monotone inverse cumulative distribution functions. In that case, inversion uses all values below the relevant quantile rather than, for instance, the value at the first crossing. With Estimator.POSITIVE, the weights are projected on the outcome and treatment, which makes them nonnegative.
The framework requires a binary treatment and a binary instrument.
Standard errors are computed via the case bootstrap.

import time

Show code (Python defining the comparison-table helpers)
def make_source_note(n_obs: int, n_iter: int, n_workers: int) -> str:
    return (
        f"N = {int(n_obs):,}; {int(n_iter):,} bootstrap iterations; "
        f"{int(n_workers)} workers for parallel computations."
    )


def make_timing_table(ds: pl.DataFrame, estimation: str, source_note: str) -> GT:
    return (
        GT(ds.select("package", "computation", "seconds"))
        .cols_label(package="Package", computation="Computation", seconds="Seconds")
        .fmt_number(columns=["seconds"], decimals=1, use_seps=True)
        .tab_header(title=md("**Speed Comparison**"), subtitle=estimation)
        .tab_source_note(source_note)
    )


def make_comparison_data(qs, series) -> pl.DataFrame:
    """Tidy estimate/SE data for a package-vs-package comparison.

    ``series`` maps a ``(package, computation)`` label to an ``(effects, ses)``
    pair, each ordered as ``[QTE(q) for q in qs] + [ATT]``.
    """
    n_qte = len(qs)
    records = []
    for (package, computation), (effects, ses) in series.items():
        for i, q in enumerate(qs):  # quantiles
            records.append(
                {
                    "effect": "QTE",
                    "quantile": f"{q:.2f}",
                    "package": package,
                    "computation": computation,
                    "estimate": float(effects[i]),
                    "se": float(ses[i]),
                }
            )
        records.append(
            {
                "effect": "ATT",
                "quantile": "",
                "package": package,
                "computation": computation,
                "estimate": float(effects[n_qte]),
                "se": float(ses[n_qte]),
            }
        )
    return pl.DataFrame(records)


def make_estimate_comparison_table(data: pl.DataFrame, estimation: str, source_note: str) -> GT:
    """Render tidy comparison data (see ``make_comparison_data``).

    Rows are grouped under ``QTE``/``ATT``; package names become the top-level
    column spanners with the computation nested underneath. Estimate and
    standard-error columns get distinct backgrounds, and packages are separated
    by a vertical rule.
    """
    pairs = data.select("package", "computation").unique(maintain_order=True).rows()
    packages = list(dict.fromkeys(package for package, _ in pairs))
    computations = list(dict.fromkeys(computation for _, computation in pairs))

    def series(package, computation):
        # filter preserves the QTE...ATT order produced by make_comparison_data
        return data.filter((pl.col("package") == package) & (pl.col("computation") == computation))

    base = series(*pairs[0])
    frame = {"effect": base["effect"].to_list(), "quantile": base["quantile"].to_list()}
    leaf_labels = {}
    for package, computation in pairs:
        prefix = f"{package}.{computation}"
        sub = series(package, computation)
        frame[f"{prefix}.est"] = sub["estimate"].to_list()
        frame[f"{prefix}.se"] = sub["se"].to_list()
        leaf_labels[f"{prefix}.est"] = "Estimate"
        leaf_labels[f"{prefix}.se"] = md("Standard<br>Error")

    table = pl.DataFrame(frame)
    est_cols = [c for c in table.columns if c.endswith(".est")]
    se_cols = [c for c in table.columns if c.endswith(".se")]

    gt = (
        GT(table, groupname_col="effect")
        .row_group_order(["QTE", "ATT"])
        .cols_label(quantile="Quantile", **leaf_labels)
        .fmt_number(columns=est_cols + se_cols, decimals=1, use_seps=True)
        .tab_header(title=md("**Results Comparison**"), subtitle=estimation)
        .tab_source_note(source_note)
        .tab_style(style=style.fill(color="#E8F1FA"), locations=loc.body(columns=est_cols))
        .tab_style(style=style.fill(color="#FBF0E1"), locations=loc.body(columns=se_cols))
        .tab_style(style=style.fill(color="#D3E4F5"), locations=loc.column_labels(columns=est_cols))
        .tab_style(style=style.fill(color="#F6E0C4"), locations=loc.column_labels(columns=se_cols))
    )
    for package in packages:
        # narrower spanners first so the package spanner sits on top
        package_columns = []
        for computation in computations:
            est_col, se_col = f"{package}.{computation}.est", f"{package}.{computation}.se"
            if est_col not in frame:
                continue
            gt = gt.tab_spanner(
                computation, columns=[est_col, se_col], id=f"{package}|{computation}"
            )
            package_columns += [est_col, se_col]
        gt = gt.tab_spanner(package, columns=package_columns, id=f"{package}|pkg")
    if len(packages) > 1:
        divider = "#8A8A8A"
        second_package = packages[1]
        first_computation = next(
            computation for package, computation in pairs if package == second_package
        )
        first_of_second = f"{second_package}.{first_computation}.est"
        gt = gt.tab_style(
            style=style.borders(sides="left", color=divider, style="solid", weight=px(2)),
            locations=[
                loc.body(columns=first_of_second),
                loc.column_labels(columns=first_of_second),
                loc.spanner_labels(ids=[f"{second_package}|pkg"]),
                loc.spanner_labels(ids=[f"{second_package}|{first_computation}"]),
            ],
        )
    return gt

title: QTE Benchmark: py-qte vs R qte
text:
Summary
Here, we compare the performance of the py-qte and the qte package. We use a medium-sized machine (see the Environment section for details). The comparisons are based on the relatively small Lalonde dataset that comes with the qte package and on a medium-sized simulated dataset inspired by this section from the documentation of the DoubleML package.
In particular, estimators that involve an outcome model are relatively computationally intensive since they involve fitting a quantile regression model on a grid of quantiles in each bootstrap run. So speed matters here.
Even for the small Lalonde dataset (2,675 observations), we find sizeable differences between the qte and the py-qte packages in sequential computations. These can be closely tied to different implementation approaches of the respective estimators. Parallelized approaches benefit qte relatively more (in this setting). See Table 2. For estimation with confounders, the same holds true, but even after parallelization the gap remains sizeable, and the qte package takes about 3 times as long as the py-qte package (see Table 4).
For a larger simulated dataset (2,000 observations), we find that without confounders py-qte is orders of magnitude as fast even after parallelization. See Table 6. For the AIPW estimator we find that the parallelized py-qte version on a medium-sized dataset (2,000 observations and 5 covariates) with a reasonable number of bootstrap iterations is more than 20 times faster than the qte version. See Table 9.
Lastly, the py-qte version can provide results for 400 observations and 3 bootstrap iterations in about 260 seconds. This is about half the time the parallelized qte version took for a dataset that has only 20% of the rows. Interestingly, the parallelized py-qte version with 4 workers is about 10 times faster than the sequential version, which suggests that the chosen parallelization strategy based on threads is close to optimal for larger datasets. See Table 11.
Overall, these results stress the importance of algorithmic choices and parallelization strategies for the bootstrap iterations.

We further see in Table 4 that the sequential version of py-qte is much faster than the qte version. This is probably largely due to the fact that py-qte computes \(F_{AIPW}(y)\) on the y-grid in a single (vectorized) pass whereas the qte version computes each point on the y-grid separately in a loop. The parallelized version of py-qte retains a sizeable advantage over the qte version although the gap is considerably narrower than in the sequential case.

        "language": ["Python", "Python"],

AIPW Estimator 
The simulated dataset has five covariates: the outcome model uses five transformed features of them, whereas the propensity score uses three of the raw covariates. Note that qte::unc_qte takes a single xformla used for both the propensity score and the outcome regression, so the R run below fits both models on the same five features while the py-qte run uses separate formulas. The population (“true”) effects of this design are reported in Table 7. They are obtained by generating a large dataset at the true parameter values and subsequently computing the quantities of interest from that dataset.
